paragraphs.text: Form No:HCJD/C-121 ORDER SHEET IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT MULTAN BENCH MULTAN JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT Case No: W.P.No.14044/2026 United Insurance Company of Pakistan Limited Versus Dr. Asma Malik and AD & SJ/Presiding Officer District Consumer Court, Bhakkar S.No. of order/ Proceeding Date of order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of Parties or counsel, where necessary. 10.11.2026 Syed Muhammad Junaid Mumtaz, Advocate for the Petitioner. Mr. Bashir Ahmed Buzdar, Additional Advocate General (on Court call). Rana Muhammad Javaid Iqbal, Assistant Attorney General (on Court call). Through this petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (the “Constitution”), the Petitioner has called in question the vires of the impugned order dated 06.10.2026, passed by the Presiding Officer, District Consumer Court, Bhakkar (the “Consumer Court”), whereby the objection raised by it regarding maintainability of the complaint instituted by Respondent No.1 has been overruled and complaint has been held to be maintainable for the purpose of further proceedings.

At the outset, Syed Muhammad Junaid Mumtaz, Advocate contends that the Consumer Court lacks jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate upon the complaint filed by the Respondent No.1 in light of the law laid down by this Court in the case of Regional Manager, Adamjee Insurance Company Ltd. versus Presiding Officer, District Consumer Court, Lahore and 3 others (2012 CLD 846). He submits that the Consumer Court, while passing the impugned order, has failed to take into consideration the principles enunciated in the aforesaid case and, without examining the relevant statutory provisions governing the subject, merely observed that since the dispute emanates from the provision of insurance services, complaint falls within its jurisdiction. He claims that such an approach is contrary to the applicable statutory framework and the binding precedent of this Court.

The controversy raised in the instant petition involves a short question of law, which can conveniently be examined in the light of the relevant statutory provisions and the judicial precedents governing the subject. In these circumstances, issuance of notice to Respondent No.1 is dispensed with as the matter can be appropriately addressed on the basis of the available record, without causing any prejudice to the parties. The exercise is also consistent with the doctrine of limine control, recognized by this Court in the case of Asif Saleem versus Chairman BOG University of Lahore and others (PLD 2019 Lahore 407), whereby, in appropriate cases, the Court may undertake an expeditious examination and disposal of a matter at the threshold, on the basis of the material available on the record, so as to avoid unnecessary proceedings, inconvenience and expense to the parties and to advance the cause of speedy justice. The doctrine of limine control was subsequently further strengthened and followed by the Division Bench of this Court in the case of Messrs Colony Textile Mills Limited and another versus First Punjab Modaraba (2021 CLD 1212), which was, then, also relied by the Division Bench of Sindh High Court in the case of Muhammad Shehzad versus Faisal Bank Limited and another (2024 CLD 141). Subsequently, this principle has also been expanded by this Court in the cases of Sardar Qurban Ali Dogar versus Pakistan Bar Council through Chairman and 8 others (2022 CLC 646), Muhammad Tahir Pervaiz and others versus Province of Punjab and others (2022 MLD 1777), Humaira Mehboob versus Summit Bank Limited and others (2023 CLD 525) and Fahim Ahmed Saeed and others versus Mian Humayun Mahmud and others (2025 MLD 1973).

Before examining the controversy, it is appropriate to briefly examine the Preamble of the Insurance Ordinance, 2000 (the “Ordinance”). The Preamble makes clear that the Ordinance was promulgated to regulate the insurance business, ensure the protection of policyholders’ interests, promote the sound development of the industry and provide for ancillary matters. The policy holder is defined under Section 2(xivi) of the Ordinance as a person to whom a policy is issued or, in the case of a policy of life insurance, the person to whom the whole of the interest of the policy holder in the policy is assigned once and for all, but does not include an assignee thereof whose interest in the policy is defeasible or is for the time being subject to any condition.

Now, turning to the substantive provisions governing the adjudication of disputes within this statutory framework, Section of Ordinance assumes particular significance. For ease of reference, the relevant provisions are reproduced below: “122. Powers of Tribunal.- (1) A Tribunal shall: (a) in the exercise of its civil jurisdiction, have in respect of a claim filed by a policy holder against an insurance company in respect of, or arising out of a policy of insurance, all the powers vested in a civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908); (b) ------------------------------------- (c) ------------------------------------- (d) ------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------- No Court other than a Tribunal shall have or exercise any jurisdiction with respect to any matter to which the jurisdiction of a Tribunal extends under this Ordinance, including a decision as to the territorial limits and the execution of a decree, order or judgment passed by a Tribunal: Provided that for the purposes of this section a Small Claims Settlement Committee established under section 117 shall not be deemed to be a Court.” A plain reading of Section 122(1)(a), when considered in conjunction with Section 122(3) of the Ordinance, makes it evident that the legislature has vested the Tribunal, which is established under Section 121 of the Ordinance, with exclusive jurisdiction in respect of claims falling within the specified statutory domain, namely, claims instituted by a policyholder against an insurance company in respect of, or arising out of, an insurance policy. The expression employed in Section 122(3) expressly excludes the jurisdiction of any other Court in respect of matters falling within the jurisdiction conferred upon the Tribunal under the Ordinance. Thus, where a claim squarely falls within the scope of Section 122(1)(a), its adjudication must take place before the forum designated under the Ordinance, to the exclusion of any other Court. The mere characterization of a dispute as one relating to the provision of services, therefore, cannot, by itself, confer jurisdiction upon the Consumer Court where the subject matter of the claim is otherwise governed by the exclusive jurisdictional regime prescribed under Ordinance. 6. The aforesaid statutory position has also been examined by this Court in Regional Manager Case , Adamjee Insurance Company Ltd. versus Presiding Officer, District Consumer Court, Lahore and 3 others (2012 CLD 846), wherein, after considering the relevant provisions of the Ordinance, it was held that a claim instituted by a policyholder against an insurance company before the Consumer Court, falling within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal under the Ordinance, was not maintainable before the Consumer Court. This Court further observed that, in view of Article 143 of the Constitution, the provisions of competent federal legislation would prevail over any inconsistent provincial legislation. It was also recognized that where a special enactment provides a specific mechanism for adjudication of disputes relating to a particular subject, the general law cannot be invoked to displace the jurisdiction conferred upon the specialized forum by such enactment. Thereafter, in the case of Messrs Sui Northern Gas Pipeline Limited through General Manager and 2 others versus Abdul Hameed (2012 CLD 1428), this Court has further clarified that: “…No doubt no objection was raised at the instance of present appellants questioning the jurisdiction of consumer Court but since the consumer Court is not a Court of general jurisdiction, therefore, it was its duty to examine the allegations contained in the complaint in order to determine its jurisdiction. Prayer for cancellation of sui gas bill and change of meter by no stretch of imagination could have conferred jurisdiction upon the consumer Court as the same falls outside the purview of consumer Court. Keeping in view the allegations and relief sought for consumer Court was not vested with any jurisdiction to take the cognizance of grievance of respondent and as such while accepting the appeal, order dated 2- 5-2008 is hereby set aside resulting in dismissal of complaint filed by respondent leaving the parties to bear their own costs.” The issue regarding the jurisdiction of a Consumer Court was also addressed in the judgment reported as FESCO and others versus Sh. Jamil Ahmad (2016 CLC 1104) wherein this Court observed that jurisdiction of Consumer Court is restricted to the extent of defective product or service for which a consumer could file a claim to recover damages against the manufacturer or service provider. In the said judgment, it was also held that the Consumer Court lacks the jurisdiction to issue an injunction against the Respondent and set aside the impugned order being legally untenable. Reference can also be made to the dictum laid down in the case of S.E. MEPCO and others versus Judge District Consumer Court and another (PLD 2019 Lahore 165) in which this Court has examined the scope of the Consumer Court's jurisdiction and held that the Consumer Court is duty bound to determine its own jurisdiction at the outset.

Similarly, in the judgment reported as Messrs Bahria Town (Pvt.) Ltd. through Manager (Operations) versus District Consumer Court, Rawalpindi and 2 others (PLD 2022 Lahore 488), a Division Bench of this Court (Rawalpindi Bench), while examining the jurisdiction of the Consumer Court in the context of disputes arising out of the terms and conditions governing the sale and purchase of immovable property, held that such disputes, in the circumstances considered therein, could not be adjudicated upon by the Consumer Court. The said judgment reinforces the principle that the jurisdiction of a Consumer Court cannot be assumed merely on the basis of the nature or description of the transaction rather, the nature of the claim, the applicable statutory framework and jurisdiction expressly conferred upon the relevant forum must be examined.

In view of the foregoing statutory provisions and judicial pronouncements, it was incumbent upon the Consumer Court to examine the objection regarding its jurisdiction and maintainability of the complaint in the light of Section 122(1)(a) read with Section 122(3) of the Ordinance, as well as the principles enunciated in the aforesaid judgments of this Court. The question could not have been answered merely by observing that the complaint relates to the provision of insurance services. The Consumer Court was required to determine, by examining the substance of the allegations, the nature of the relief claimed and the relationship between the parties, whether the claim instituted by the Respondent No.1 is, in essence, a claim by a policyholder against an insurance company in respect of, or arising out of, an insurance policy, and consequently falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal under the Ordinance.

For what has been discussed above, this petition is allowed. The impugned order dated 06.10.2026, passed by the Presiding Officer, District Consumer Court, Bhakkar, is set aside only to the extent of the determination of the question of maintainability of the complaint instituted by the Respondent No.1. The matter is remanded to the Consumer Court with the direction to decide the question of maintainability afresh, strictly in accordance with law, after examining relevant provisions of the Ordinance, particularly Sections 122(1)(a) and 122(3) thereof, and keeping in view the principles laid down by this Court in the aforesaid cases, through a speaking order, without being influenced by its earlier findings on the question of maintainability, within a period of one month from the date of receipt of certified copy of this order. (JAWAD HASSAN) JUDGE APPROVED FOR REPORTING JUDGE *Mãjîd
